pages.title: One element can have more than one oxidation state

blocks.text: Iron forms both FeCl₂ and FeCl₃. Saying iron chloride alone leaves the oxidation state unclear. Stock notation makes the distinction visible and also helps identify which state changes during reaction.
Stock notation uses a Roman numeral for oxidation state, as in iron(II) chloride and iron(III) chloride. It refers to the metal state, not the number of atoms in a formula.

pages.transition: Use the oxidation-state change to identify a redox reaction.

pages.title: Increasing oxidation number means oxidation

blocks.text: Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number; reduction is a decrease. Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ is oxidation from +2 to +3. Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺ is reduction.
In 2Cu₂O + Cu₂S → 6Cu + SO₂, copper goes from +1 to 0 and is reduced. Sulfur goes from −2 to +4 and is oxidised. Six copper atoms each gain one bookkeeping electron while sulfur loses six.

pages.transition: The reaction’s pattern gives a second useful classification.

pages.title: Combination reactions can be redox

blocks.text: A combination reaction joins reactants into a product. It is redox when oxidation states change, such as elements forming a compound. The pattern alone is not sufficient evidence.
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO combines elements: Mg changes 0 → +2 and O changes 0 → −2. But CaO + CO₂ → CaCO₃ is combination without changes in Ca(+2), C(+4) or O(−2).
Classify by calculating states on both sides rather than assuming every combination is oxidation.

pages.transition: The reverse structural pattern is decomposition.

pages.title: Decomposition is not automatically redox

blocks.text: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂ is redox: Cl changes +5 → −1 and O changes −2 → 0. One element is reduced while another is oxidised.
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ is decomposition but not redox, because all oxidation states remain unchanged. A reaction breaking one substance into several does not itself prove electron redistribution.

pages.transition: Displacement compares an element with a related ion or compound.

pages.title: Metal displacement couples two state changes

blocks.text: In displacement, one element replaces another in a compound or ionic solution. A more effective reducing metal can reduce ions of another metal under suitable conditions.
Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu: Zn changes 0 → +2 and Cu +2 → 0. Zinc displaces copper. Spectator counterions do not need to appear in the net ionic equation.

pages.transition: Non-metal displacement follows the same coupled logic.

pages.title: Hydrogen and halogen displacement

blocks.text: Zn + 2H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + H₂ displaces hydrogen. Zinc loses two electrons while two protons gain them. For Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, chlorine is reduced and bromide is oxidised.
The reducing or oxidising strength determines which displacement is favoured. The position of a symbol in the periodic table alone should not replace the relevant chemical conditions.

pages.transition: Sometimes one element in one reactant undergoes both changes.

pages.title: Recognise disproportionation

blocks.text: Disproportionation occurs when the same element in one reactant is simultaneously oxidised and reduced to different product states. Its initial state must allow both an increase and a decrease.
In 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂, oxygen begins at −1. Some becomes −2 in water and some becomes 0 in O₂. Hydrogen stays +1, so oxygen supplies both redox roles.

pages.transition: A contrasting example helps avoid over-classifying a reaction.

pages.title: A redox change can cross within one compound

blocks.text: In a decomposition such as 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂, different elements change: Cl is reduced and O is oxidised. It is redox decomposition, but not disproportionation of one element.

Disproportionation requires the same element to appear in both a higher and lower product state than its single initial state. Merely having oxidation and reduction in the same equation is not enough.

pages.transition: Practise a full classification using oxidation-state sums.

pages.title: Worked reaction classification

blocks.text: Teacher-created check: 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃. In FeCl₂, Fe is +2; in FeCl₃ it is +3, so two Fe atoms each lose one electron. Cl₂ begins at 0 and becomes chloride at −1, gaining two electrons in total. Cl₂ is the oxidant; Fe(II) is the reductant.
Naming both agents and counting the changes verifies the redox assignment. Stock numerals identify the changing metal states without altering the chemical formulas.
An element in its highest oxidation state cannot be oxidised further within the available ordinary states; this helps screen possible disproportionation candidates.

pages.transition: Revise classification using state changes rather than equation shape alone.

pages.title: Revision: patterns help, oxidation states decide

blocks.text: Stock Roman numerals identify oxidation states. An increase is oxidation and a decrease is reduction. Combination, decomposition and displacement can be redox, but verify state changes before applying the label.
Disproportionation is the special case where one element in one reactant is both oxidised and reduced. Match total state increases and decreases, and identify the oxidant as the species reduced.

questions.question: What does iron(III) mean?
questions.answer: Iron has oxidation state +3; the numeral is not the number of iron atoms.

questions.question: Is CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ redox?
questions.answer: No. Ca remains +2, carbon +4 and oxygen −2.

questions.question: In 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃, what is the oxidising agent?
questions.answer: Cl₂; chlorine is reduced from 0 to −1.

questions.question: Why is hydrogen peroxide decomposition disproportionation?
questions.answer: Oxygen at −1 forms both oxygen at −2 in water and oxygen at 0 in O₂.

questions.question: Does every decomposition involve disproportionation?
questions.answer: No. Even a redox decomposition can oxidise and reduce different elements rather than the same one.

questions.question: How many electrons are gained by the six Cu atoms in 2Cu₂O + Cu₂S → 6Cu + SO₂?
questions.answer: Each Cu goes from +1 to 0 and gains one, giving six bookkeeping electrons in total.
